newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end higher but dollar-linked down.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end higher but dollar-linked down.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed generally higher on Wednesday but dollar-linked bonds fell for the second day as the shekel gained on the U.S. currency, traders said.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.09 pct to 107.40
Volume including Makams was 214 million shekels, with turnover in dollar-linked bonds at 14 million shekels.

"CPI-linked bonds, especially short-term bonds, rose today on expectations of higher inflation in the coming months, but unlinked bonds also rose on expectations that interest rates will remain stable despite the higher inflation," said Roy Meir of Simodan.

Dollar-linked bonds fell as the U.S. currency dropped another notch against the shekel, he added. The shekel rose 1.2 percent to 3.5050 against the dollar on Wednesday bringing the currency's gain to a total of 2.4 percent since Friday.
The shekel tumbled five percent in the last week of June after the government instituted changes in the exchange rate mechanism and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates 1.2 percentage points.

The soaring dollar had caused prices of unlinked bonds to fall while prices of CPI-linked short bonds rose on fears of higher inflation. But Meir said the resulting uncertainty that had prevailed in the market was now over.

"There is a consensus that the dollar will stabilise at 3.50 shekels, which is a level good for everyone," Meir said. "The dollar's rise is expected to influence the June, July and August consumer price indices by a total of 0.5 percent, which is reasonable."

"The market has gone back to where it was before the exchange rate reform and the cut in interest rates," said Baruch Glicksberg, an institutional investor. "The hysterical fear of a depreciation doesn't exist anymore."
Yields on CPI-linked short bonds were 4.2 percent while on CPI-linked long bonds they were 4.1 percent, he said. Yields on one-year unlinked bonds and Makams were around 13 percent, he said.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
